prompt: To determine whether the kind of seed influences the height of the seedlings, the experimenters should most likely:

choices.text: Vary the kind of seed while holding the fertilizer concentration and all other conditions constant
choices.rationale: Correct. To test a new factor, change only that factor and hold everything else, including the original independent variable, constant.

choices.text: Vary both the kind of seed and the fertilizer concentration at the same time in each trial, measuring the height of the seedlings
choices.rationale: Changing two factors at once makes it impossible to tell which one caused any change.

choices.text: Repeat Experiment 1 exactly as before, but with a larger number of values of the fertilizer concentration
choices.rationale: This gives more detail about fertilizer concentration but never changes the kind of seed.

choices.text: Measure the kind of seed in each trial of Experiment 1 instead of measuring the height of the seedlings
choices.rationale: Measuring the kind of seed does not test its effect; it must be deliberately varied.

explanation: A fair test of the kind of seed changes it alone. The fertilizer concentration, which was the variable in Experiment 1, must now be held fixed.

table.caption: Experiment 1: Students planted bean seeds in identical pots of potting soil and watered each pot with 100 mL of fertilizer solution every other day. After 4 weeks they measured the height of each seedling. Each concentration was tested with five pots, and the average height was recorded. Table 1 lists the results.

prompt: Based on Experiments 1 and 2, is the claim that the volume of water affects the boiling point of the water supported?

choices.text: Yes; the boiling point of the water was higher for 1000 mL than for 500 mL at every altitude
choices.rationale: The two columns are identical, so neither condition gave higher values.

choices.text: Yes; the boiling point of the water decreased as altitude increased in both experiments
choices.rationale: That trend concerns altitude, not the volume of water, and appears identically in both experiments.

choices.text: No; the boiling point of the water did not change with altitude in either experiment
choices.rationale: The boiling point of the water did change with altitude; the point is that the condition made no difference.

choices.text: No; at every altitude tested, the two experiments gave the same boiling point
choices.rationale: Correct. Changing the condition left every result unchanged, so the results give no sign that it matters.

explanation: Experiments 1 and 2 differ only in the volume of water, and every value is the same in both, so the results do not support the claim.

table.caption: Experiment 1: A team carried the same kettle, thermometer, and a measured volume of distilled water to stations at several altitudes using 500 mL of water. At each station the water was heated until it boiled steadily and the temperature was recorded. Experiment 2: The procedure was repeated using 1000 mL of water, with everything else unchanged. Table 1 lists the results of both experiments.

prompt: Which experiment(s) provide the information needed to determine whether the inside temperature affects the rate of heat loss?

choices.text: Experiment 2 alone, because it was the only experiment performed at 80°C
choices.rationale: Experiment 2 also used only one setting of the inside temperature; a comparison is required.

choices.text: Experiment 1 alone, because it tested the full range of the thickness of the insulation under one condition
choices.rationale: Experiment 1 used a single setting of the inside temperature, so by itself it cannot reveal its effect.

choices.text: Neither experiment, because the thickness of the insulation was varied in both of them
choices.rationale: Varying insulation thickness in both experiments is what makes them comparable row by row; the comparison across experiments is exactly what is needed.

choices.text: Experiments 1 and 2 together, because they differ only in the inside temperature
choices.rationale: Correct. Only by comparing results obtained under the two conditions, with everything else the same, can the effect of that condition be isolated.

explanation: Each experiment holds the inside temperature fixed at one setting; the two settings differ between experiments, so comparing Experiments 1 and 2 isolates its effect.

stimulus.title: Insulation and Heat Loss
stimulus.text:
Experiment 1
Students wrapped a metal box containing an electric heater in foam sheets of a set total thickness. They adjusted the heater power until the inside temperature held steady at 60°C in a 20°C room and recorded that power as the rate of heat loss.
Results (the rate of heat loss): at 0 cm, 127 W; at 2 cm, 74 W; at 4 cm, 52 W; at 6 cm, 41 W; at 8 cm, 33 W; at 10 cm, 28 W.

Experiment 2
The procedure of Experiment 1 was repeated at 80°C, with everything else unchanged.
Results: at 0 cm, 184 W; at 2 cm, 108 W; at 4 cm, 76 W; at 6 cm, 59 W; at 8 cm, 48 W; at 10 cm, 40 W.

prompt: Suppose Experiment 1 were repeated with a water bath at 25°C, a setting between those used in Experiments 1 and 2. At a catalyst mass of 10 mg, the time for the reaction to finish would most likely be:

choices.text: above both experiments' results, greater than 24 s
choices.rationale: This is above both experiments' results at this row; an intermediate setting should not fall outside them.

choices.text: below both experiments' results, less than 13 s
choices.rationale: This is below both experiments' results at this row; an intermediate setting should not fall outside them.

choices.text: between 17 s and 32 s
choices.rationale: These are the results for 8 mg, not 10 mg.

choices.text: between 13 s and 24 s
choices.rationale: Correct. At 10 mg, Experiment 1 gave 24 and Experiment 2 gave 13; an intermediate setting should give an intermediate result.

explanation: The two experiments bracket the new setting, so the result at 10 mg should lie between 13 and 24 s.

table.caption: Experiment 1: Students mixed 50 mL of hydrogen peroxide solution from a single bottle with a measured mass of powdered catalyst in a water bath at 20°C and timed how long it took for the bubbling to stop. Experiment 2: The procedure was repeated in a water bath at 30°C, with everything else unchanged. Table 1 lists the results of both experiments.

choices.text: Repeat Experiment 1 exactly as before, but with a larger number of values of the light intensity
choices.rationale: This gives more detail about light intensity but never changes the counting time.

choices.text: Vary both the counting time and the light intensity at the same time in each trial, measuring the rate of photosynthesis
choices.rationale: Changing two factors at once makes it impossible to tell which one caused any change.

choices.text: Measure the counting time in each trial of Experiment 1 instead of measuring the rate of photosynthesis
choices.rationale: Measuring the counting time does not test its effect; it must be deliberately varied.

choices.text: Vary the counting time while holding the light intensity and all other conditions constant
choices.rationale: Correct. To test a new factor, change only that factor and hold everything else, including the original independent variable, constant.

table.caption: Experiment 1: Students placed a sprig of pondweed in a test tube of water and set a lamp at distances giving several light intensities. They counted the oxygen bubbles released in one minute at each intensity, repeating each count three times. Table 1 lists the results.

prompt: Based on Experiments 1 and 2, is the claim that the month of the measurements affects the water temperature supported?

choices.text: No; the two experiments gave the same temperature at every depth tested
choices.rationale: The columns differ at every depth; compare them row by row.

choices.text: No; the water temperature decreased as depth increased in both experiments
choices.rationale: A shared trend with depth says nothing about whether the month of the measurements matters; the two columns differ at every row.

choices.text: Yes; the water temperature decreased as depth increased in both Experiment 1 and Experiment 2
choices.rationale: That trend concerns depth, not the month of the measurements; it would appear even if the condition had no effect.

choices.text: Yes; at every depth tested, the water temperature was higher for July than for September
choices.rationale: Correct. The two experiments differ only in this condition, and the results differ consistently between them.

explanation: Because the experiments differ only in the month of the measurements, the consistent gap between the two sets of results (higher for July) shows that the condition affects the water temperature.

table.caption: Experiment 1: From a boat anchored over the deepest part of a lake in July, students lowered a thermometer probe on a marked cable and recorded the water temperature at several depths. All readings were taken within one hour at midday. Experiment 2: The procedure was repeated in September, with everything else unchanged. Table 1 lists the results of both experiments.

prompt: To decide whether the tire used has an effect on the tire pressure, a student should compare the results of:

choices.text: Experiment 2 alone, because it was the only experiment performed using Tire B, inflated to a higher starting pressure
choices.rationale: Experiment 2 also used only one setting of the tire used; a comparison is required.

choices.text: Neither experiment, because the air temperature was varied in both of them
choices.rationale: Varying temperature in both experiments is what makes them comparable row by row; the comparison across experiments is exactly what is needed.

choices.text: Experiments 1 and 2 together, because they differ only in the tire used
choices.rationale: Correct. Only by comparing results obtained under the two conditions, with everything else the same, can the effect of that condition be isolated.

choices.text: Experiment 1 alone, because it tested the full range of the air temperature under one condition
choices.rationale: Experiment 1 used a single setting of the tire used, so by itself it cannot reveal its effect.

explanation: Each experiment holds the tire used fixed at one setting; the two settings differ between experiments, so comparing Experiments 1 and 2 isolates its effect.

stimulus.title: Temperature and Tire Pressure
stimulus.text:
Experiment 1
A sealed bicycle tire was placed in a chamber using Tire A whose temperature could be set. At each temperature the tire was left for 30 minutes and its pressure was then read with a gauge.
Results (the tire pressure): at 10 °C, 217.4 kPa; at 20 °C, 225.1 kPa; at 30 °C, 232.8 kPa; at 40 °C, 240.5 kPa; at 50 °C, 248.1 kPa.

Experiment 2
The procedure of Experiment 1 was repeated using Tire B, inflated to a higher starting pressure, with everything else unchanged.
Results: at 10 °C, 312.3 kPa; at 20 °C, 323.3 kPa; at 30 °C, 334.3 kPa; at 40 °C, 345.3 kPa; at 50 °C, 356.4 kPa.

prompt: If a third experiment used a temperature of 30°C and all other conditions of Experiments 1 and 2, the activity of the enzyme at pH 5 would most likely be:

choices.text: between 65 µmol/min and 92 µmol/min
choices.rationale: These are the results for pH 6, not pH 5.

choices.text: between 45 µmol/min and 63 µmol/min
choices.rationale: Correct. At pH 5, Experiment 1 gave 45 and Experiment 2 gave 63; an intermediate setting should give an intermediate result.

choices.text: above both experiments' results, greater than 63 µmol/min
choices.rationale: This is above both experiments' results at this row; an intermediate setting should not fall outside them.

choices.text: below both experiments' results, less than 45 µmol/min
choices.rationale: This is below both experiments' results at this row; an intermediate setting should not fall outside them.

explanation: The two experiments bracket the new setting, so the result at pH 5 should lie between 45 and 63 µmol/min.

table.caption: Experiment 1: Students added 1 mL of enzyme solution to tubes containing a substrate solution buffered to a set pH and kept the tubes at 25°C. They measured how much product formed in 5 minutes to find the activity. Each pH was tested in triplicate. Experiment 2: The procedure was repeated and kept the tubes at 35°C, with everything else unchanged. Table 1 lists the results of both experiments.

table.caption: Experiment 1: Students spread 0.1 mL of a bacterial culture onto agar plates containing a known concentration of an antibiotic. After 24 hours they counted the colonies on each plate. Three plates were prepared for each concentration and the average count was recorded. Table 1 lists the results.

table.caption: Experiment 1: Students hung a metal bob from a string using a 50 g bob, pulled the bob 10° to one side, and released it. They timed 10 complete swings with a stopwatch and divided by 10 to find the period. The procedure was repeated for several string lengths. Experiment 2: The procedure was repeated using a 100 g bob, with everything else unchanged. Table 1 lists the results of both experiments.

stimulus.title: Solubility and Temperature
stimulus.text:
Experiment 1
Students heated 100 g of distilled water to a set temperature in a beaker using Salt A and added the salt one gram at a time, stirring after each addition, until no more would dissolve. They recorded the total mass dissolved at each temperature.
Results (the mass of salt that dissolved): at 0 °C, 16 g; at 20 °C, 29 g; at 40 °C, 52 g; at 60 °C, 86 g; at 80 °C, 130 g.

Experiment 2
The procedure of Experiment 1 was repeated using Salt B, with everything else unchanged.
Results: at 0 °C, 12 g; at 20 °C, 21 g; at 40 °C, 38 g; at 60 °C, 63 g; at 80 °C, 96 g.
